title: Paradox Bloom
logline: BaneWAP seizes the egg and wishes huge — and the wish grants at once, minimum-viable, an empire hollow as a rented crown.
epigraph: A grand wish grants easily. It is the finishing that never comes.
description: Chapter 11 of Lore.Land: Paradox Bloom. BaneWAP snatches the unspent wish and wishes an empire; karmic momentum obliges one coincidence at a time, delivering it mediocre and hollow. Bloom arrives before seed, his hoarded berries wake inside him, and the egg — unfinished, unfinishable — rolls back warm to Boof's paws.

content.text: Below Bone.land the road ran through an old bloom garden nobody had kept for years. Quince had gone to riot over the walls, the blackthorn hedge stood white with flower, and a moss-thick sundial pointed at the wrong hour without minding. Boof smelled sap, sloe-blossom, {{garden-scent}}. Then cold pastry.

old brick warming under the quince

content.text: It happened between one honest sniff and the next. Where the frame's note still hung in the air, Mr. BaneWAP stopped shadowing and simply took — banker's crust cracking with the effort, tin lockbox open and shut, the egg gone from Boof's sling before her growl could finish forming. He did not run far. He did not need to.

“Behold!” he announced to the bloom garden, which had not asked. “A wish the size of an empire, spent all at once, and not one clause about giving it back.” There was a clause. There is always a clause. He had written it himself, at the bottom, very small, and he never read the bottom of anything.

All around the rise, on the shut quince buds, the early bees were already waiting. They come a week before the blossom and hum at closed petals as if the bloom owed them. Boof had always thought it a poor way to spend a spring.

He had been saying it for a week, to anyone who would stand still: an empire, whole, at once. That is how a baneberry foretells, and he was made of them. Say a thing that will go wrong often enough, and loudly enough, and the world begins arranging itself to have heard you. Boof had smelled it on the wheel-tracks all the way down from the pass: not the crust, the saying, cold and plum-dark and sure of itself. Nobody had stepped on it in time.

He stood on a low rise with the warm shell in both crimped hands and wished the wish he had been drafting since the auction failed: an empire, whole, at once. And the wish — this is the part no one had priced — granted instantly. It was a moment of

children.text: . Every bud in the garden opened at once, for him, with a sound like a drawer pulled out. The early bees went in and came straight out again. A flower opened on demand has not had time to fill.

content.text: Over the wall came the beekeeper whose skeps stood along its foot, her veil half on. Her bees were walking the open petals and coming away with nothing. She looked at the flowers, and at the pie on the rise, and said to nobody who would listen, “Open nothing before it has filled.” Then she went down the row stopping each skep door with a twist of grass, so her bees would stay home until there was something to fetch. It has been the beekeepers’ rule ever since.

Karmic momentum does not refuse a grand wish. It simply pays it out the way momentum pays everything: one coincidence at a time, minimum-viable, corrections deferred. A {{coincidence-deed}} blew against his crust. A road bent to end at his feet. A distant clerk misfiled a fortune in his name. The empire arrived. It arrived mediocre.

It arrived in pieces. The throne came first, shed at the garden gate by a players' wagon that hit a rut at the convenient moment — a stage prop, gilt over pine. The throne smelled rented: {{rented-smell}} and other people's sitting. Banners came after, lifted off a dyer's line by an obliging gust, in colors nobody had ordered. Subjects arrived halfway through errands. One still held a loaf.
Boof watched the new emperor wait for the scene to feel complete. It kept arriving. It never did.

The crown came last, as crowns do. The wish did not make one; it found one. All spring the crown-wasps had been building in the blackthorn — grey paper chewed from fence rails and old auction notices, ribbed and turreted and very fine — and the nearest of their crowns came loose and settled on his crust. It was beautiful. It was hollow. It was still occupied.
Boof heard it before he did: a dry, papery hum, a rented thing with tenants. Every rented crown is wasp-work, if you hold it to your ear.

content.text: Deep beneath his crust, a berry woke. The wish had passed through him, leaving its drop of light just as it had in the fields. One seam shone, then another. Warmth worked through the bitter filling. He tasted what he had kept from everyone, himself included. Sweet. It had been sweet all along. Around him, the banners {{banner-motion}}. He made a small sound the throne did nothing to support.

variants: turned their wrong colors to the light

content.text: “It was only ever rented,” he said, to nobody. Then, because a foiled pie always says one thing more than it means to: “The crown was wasps.”

Wasps know sweetness before anyone. The crown-wasps came down out of their paper crown in a slow grey trickle, walked the flaking crust where the sweet was pushing through, and drifted off toward the quince. The crown stayed on his head, empty now. It weighed exactly what it was.

content.text: The Midas touch, sampled: everything he grasped turned to more, and none of it to enough. Sound it, send it back sweeter. That is the whole law.
He tapped the rented throne once — hollow, gilt over pine — and let the note say what the timber had: interest is owed on every borrowed want.

img.alt: A hollow instant empire assembling around a bitter crusted pie whose hoarded berries wake in gold seams; the coal-dark egg still warm at the center of the grant.

sections.figcaption: Paradox Bloom: the empire arrives; the wish does not finish.

sections.title: The Wish That Would Not Finish

content.text: Here is the paradox the timber had circled without naming: a wish only leaves its shell when it is finished, and a wish the size of an empire is never finishable. There is always one more coincidence owed, one more correction pending in some far county where a stranger's luck must be bent to balance a king's. The grant kept arriving and kept not being done.
The empire stood, hollow as a rented crown, and the egg in BaneWAP's hands stayed exactly as warm as it had been in the frozen furrow — spent and unspent at once, a note held but not released.

The banners had shaken the hedges, and rehearsal moths blundered out into daylight like guests at the wrong hour, a long way from the grove. Their wings carry tomorrow's weather, a little smudged. Today they carried the empire's: rain coming on over a court with no roof, arriving in instalments.

At the edge of the new court, a woman still holding her market basket asked whether she could go home. A banner brushed her shoulder. A rehearsal moth sat on the basket handle, opening and closing the rain.

No one answered; the emperor was staring at his own hands. Boof could smell bread cooling in the basket, {{basket-loaf}} still warm on its underside, and dust rising where the throne had scraped the ground. The empire needed this woman to be a subject.
She needed to get the bread indoors before rain; she had read the moth. Boof watched her take one step backward, then another. The banner lifted, and she slipped beneath it.

His crimped hands softened. The egg slipped, tipped, rolled down the rise, past a banner dragging in the dust, through quince petals that had opened too soon. Boof stepped forward. It came to rest against her paws, warm as ever. The crack had widened enough to show gold within. She checked the shell with her nose: hot iron, sap, a little sweetened crust. Still humming. Still waiting. She left the crack alone. She had watched a whole garden opened early that morning.

That night, wherever she set the sling down, the ground beneath it was busy by morning: torch-lines bent toward the shell from every root within reach, and the frost drew back a hand's width, as if something under the loam had been given more to work with. Whatever was in the egg, it was not keeping its warmth to itself. An early bee was waiting on the sling's knot, as if the egg owed it something too. Boof let it wait.

content.text: Eight honks sounded. The ninth still sleeps in the shell. Small wishes travel farthest.
He pointed downhill, {{downhill-past}}, to two rivers that had not yet agreed to forget their springs, and Boof — who finally almost knew her want — went to meet them.

loreItems.description: A grand wish grants instantly and minimum-viable: karmic momentum pays it out one coincidence at a time, corrections deferred elsewhere.
A wish only leaves the shell when it is finished. An empire-sized wish is never finishable, so the egg survives its own spending and rolls home.
BaneWAP's hoarded berries wake inside him — a berry notices the story it is sitting inside — and he tastes his hoard for the first time in years. Sweetness is the correction.

Crown-wasps build paper crowns in the bloom garden's blackthorn, chewed from fence rails and old auction notices. BaneWAP's crown was found, not made: wasp-work, beautiful, hollow and tenanted — and the wasps left it the moment his hoard turned sweet.
Early bees wait at shut buds as if the bloom owed them. A grand wish opens every flower at once, and a flower opened on demand has nothing in it yet.
Rehearsal moths shaken from the hedge wear the empire's weather — rain over a court with no roof, arriving in instalments. A subject who reads the moth goes home with her bread.

Open nothing before it has filled: the beekeepers’ rule, learned the morning every bud in the garden opened on demand and held nothing. The beekeeper stopped her skep doors with grass so her bees stayed home until the flowers had something to give; Boof, with the egg back at her paws, left the crack alone.

table.place: The bloom garden below Bone.land, the morning a wish granted all at once. Quince has rioted over the old walls, the blackthorn hedge stands white with flower and grey with crown-wasp paper, and a moss-thick sundial points at the wrong hour without minding. Every bud is open and nothing in them is ready; on a low rise stands a throne of gilt over pine shed by a players’ wagon, ringed by banners in colours nobody ordered and subjects still halfway through their errands. It smells of sap, sloe-blossom and sun-warm straw skeps — then cold pastry, greasepaint and wasp paper.
table.light: Clean morning light that goes strange at the edges, as if the sky were being rented. By afternoon the moths’ smudged forecast comes true: rain over a court with no roof, arriving in instalments.

hooks: The players want their throne back by evening, but the grant keeps returning it to the garden gate one convenient rut at a time. Find the one coincidence that would let a throne go — somebody, somewhere, who honestly needs a chair.

A clerk far off misfiled a fortune in the emperor’s name, and the deed it belonged to blew against his crust this morning. Carry it back to the household it was meant for before the correction reaches them the slow way, one bent coincidence at a time.

The beekeeper asks the party to keep the garden shut for a week — no picking, no wishing, no shortcuts — while the flowers fill. Everyone who passes through has an excellent reason to open something now.
encounters: A deed (roll: barn, mill, orchard, quarry, pasture) blows against someone’s legs and will not come unstuck until they agree to own a little of it.
A banner in a colour nobody ordered drops over the party, and for the rest of the scene everyone in the garden treats them as subjects of the realm.
Rehearsal moths blunder out of the hedge wearing tomorrow’s weather; whoever reads the smudge right knows when the next instalment of rain will fall.
A paper crown comes loose from the blackthorn and settles on the nearest head: beautiful, hollow, and humming with tenants who leave only when the wearer does something sweet.
Early bees hang humming at something shut — a box, a door, a letter in a pocket — certain it owes them an opening.
A subject arrives halfway through an errand, still holding a loaf (roll: seed-loaf, rye cob, plaited milk-loaf, barley bannock, crust-gold oat loaf), and asks politely which way is home.

finds.use: A paper crown from the blackthorn makes strangers defer to whoever wears it, for exactly as long as it stays occupied. Hold it to your ear and you can hear it is rented; the wasps move out the moment the wearer turns sweet, and then it weighs exactly what it is.
Follow an early bee to whatever is about to open — a bud, a letter, a door, a decision. It waits there humming, and so must you: open the thing before it has filled and it holds nothing at all.
Catch one gently and read tomorrow’s weather off its wings, a little smudged. The smudge always falls across the hour you most need to know.

bracework.does: A room you can stand in for a minute, where a shut bud dreams of being honey. Step in and you can smell whether the thing you are waiting on will be worth the wait — never what it will hold, only whether it will fill.
bracework.costs: The minute is borrowed from your own patience: the next time you wait for anything, it takes a minute longer. The box runs on borrowed warmth, and the ants under the walls will notice whose.

table.question: What is your party carrying that has not filled yet — and who among you keeps wanting to open it?
